newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan seeks North Korean over fake $100 bills.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks North Korean over fake $100 bills.

text.p: Japanese police put a North Korean citizen on their nationwide wanted list on Tuesday as a suspected mastermind of the biggest U.S. dollar counterfeit case ever reported in Japan.
The move followed the arrest of six Japanese nationals on Monday on suspicion of trying to use bogus $100 notes, police in the city of Toyama on the Sea of Japan coast said.

National Police Agency officials said investigators confiscated 930 fake $100 bills from homes and offices of the six arrested Japanese, making it the largest U.S. dollar counterfeit case reported in Japan.
Police said the bogus notes are difficult to detect, although they are printed on rough paper and come with a slightly smudged printed face of Benjamin Franklin.
Police sources said the confiscated notes are similar to the "Super K" counterfeit bills which have been found in Southeast Asia and linked to North Korea.

Police said they believe North Korean national Li Yong-bok, 57, the prime suspect in the case, smuggled the notes into Japan from an unidentified foreign country. Li was also suspected of bringing in another batch of 1,000 fake $100 dollar notes, police said.
One of the Japanese arrested on Monday, Koji Iwayama, 57, owner of a seafood processing firm in Hokkaido, northern Japan, was suspected of trying to distribute the fake dollar notes, police said.

Iwayama and the other five attempted to sell the fake notes to the owner of a construction company in Omiya, north of Tokyo. The manager tried to deposit the notes in a local bank but they were rejected, police said.

The latest arrests follow a series of counterfeiting cases linked to cash-strapped North Korea, all involving fake $100 bills. North Korea has repeatedly denied involvement in past U.S.-dollar counterfeiting crimes.
In the Super-K bill case last year, former Japanese Red Army member Yoshimi Tanaka was arrested for the attempted use of counterfeit U.S. currency in Pattaya, Thailand.
Police say the Super K bills are so called as they are an upgraded version of counterfeit notes believed to have originated in North Korea in 1980s. The K stands for Korea.
Tanaka, who fled to North Korea in 1970 after his guerrilla group hijacked a Japan Airlines plane, was travelling with a North Korean diplomatic passport when arrested.
A U.S. expert said at Tanaka's ongoing trial in Thailand that the fake dollar bills Tanaka allegedly passed in Thailand were the same as bogus notes found in a Macau bank in 1994.

Five North Koreans were arrested on suspicion of depositing fake bills with a total face value of $250,000 in the 1994 Macau case. It was later discovered that the bank held fake dollars totalling $600,000.

Last December, a North Korean diplomat was arrested in the Mongolian capital Ulan Bator on suspicion of swindling moneychangers by trying to exchange $100,000 in fake $100 notes. The diplomat was deported.

In June 1996, Russian customs officials in the port Nakhodka in the Russian far east found 100 fake $100 notes in cash held by a Russian trader, according to Interfax news agency. The trader said he received the notes from a North Korean firm in exchange for an old Russian trawler.

Analysts say Japan could become a hot spot for dollar counterfeiters especially after next April, when a newly deregulated foreign exchange law will allow small shops and convenience stores to exchange currencies.
